turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Hale? Come through. Sorry about the wait, the spirometry room was running behind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, well, I've been sitting out there since half past. I'm buggered already.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): I know. I'll be quick with the numbers, then Dr Shah will see you. Blood pressure was one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse ninety-two, oxygen sats ninety-four on air, and you were breathing about twenty a minute. Temp was normal, thirty-six point eight.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sats ninety-four. That good or what?

[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Dr Shah will talk you through it. Your spirometry, the blow test: FEV1 was one point six two litres, that's fifty-eight percent predicted, FVC two point nine litres, and the ratio fifty-six percent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Felt like I was gonna pass out doing that. Stupid test.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day, I'm Dr Shah. You look done in. What's been the main trouble?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Cough. Every morning, like clockwork. Hack hack hack. And I'm puffed doing nothing much.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the cough, in your own words. How long's it been carrying on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um... I don't know. Months. Since winter? Or before winter. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. The GP referral in front of me says the cough has been six weeks.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks? Look, that's not right. It's been way longer than six weeks. Months. I told him that.

[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. So the letter says six weeks, you're saying several months, and you can't pin the start. I'll note it as somewhere between six weeks and several months, yeah? We won't fight the calendar.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Whatever. It's been ages.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the breathlessness, how's that showing up for you?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Walking. Up the hill to the shops, I'm stopping. Even taking the bins out. Sitting down I'm alright.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any whistling or wheeze in the chest?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't wheeze.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about phlegm, anything coming up?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings, yeah. Bit of grey muck. Not much. Disgusting, I know.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Fevers?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. No temperature now. I was crook a few weeks back though, proper chest infection.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): What happened with that?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): GP said chest infection, put me on amoxicillin, three times a day for a week. Finished them, I reckon, last Tuesday. The green stuff dried up. This morning cough didn't.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Green phlegm with the infection, and that's gone?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the green's gone. Back to the grey in the mornings.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are you with the smokes? Still going?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten a day. That's all.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ten. For how long have you been a smoker?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was sixteen. I'm sixty-one, so you do the maths. And... look, it's not ten. Maybe twenty. Some days more if I'm stressed. I cut it down in my head, alright?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hear you. No lecture. What are you using for the lungs, any puffers?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue puffer. Ventolin. Two puffs when I'm gasping. Been living on it this month.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): And a preventer? Sometimes people have a purple one.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the purple inhaler. Don't ask me the name, I just call it the purple one. Chemist said it's the preventer.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): That purple preventer is usually two puffs twice a day. Is that how you're taking it?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): God, no. Maybe two puffs, might be one, I never look. And only when I remember. Couple of times a week, if that.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So we're a bit in the dark on the exact dose, and it's not being used the way these usually are.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I hate the taste. Makes me cough more. So I skip it.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Before I examine you, anything with the waterworks or the bowels? Weight dropping off?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Waterworks are fine, bowels are fine. Weight's the same. I'm just tired all the time, which doesn't help my mood, sorry if I'm snappy.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Actually, wait. You asked about wheezing. At night, when I lie down, it does whistle. I can hear it. Wakes me up some nights. I don't know why I said no.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's useful, thank you. Lying flat, night-time wheeze. We'll count that as real.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mind if we park the medicine for a tick? I drove in past the MCG and the whole city's still arguing about that last over.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't start me. Starc was robbed. The review was a joke.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): I thought the third umpire bottled it. My brother-in-law hasn't shut up since Sunday.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): We had the telly on at the pub. Bloke next to me nearly threw his beer. Then the rain delay, typical Melbourne.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): That storm came out of nowhere. I got soaked just getting from the car park.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah the freeway was a car park too. Monash was dead from Chadstone. Took me forty minutes to do nothing.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you see the kid they interviewed, the one in the baggy green pyjamas?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): That was my neighbour's grandson, I swear he looked just like him. Not actually him. Cute though. Kid was waving a plastic bat in the rain.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Made my day, that bit. Right. Sorry. Back to your chest, if you're ready.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): About time. My back's killing me on this chair. Wait, no, not killing me, the chair's just hard. Don't write that down.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't. Can I have a listen to your chest?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Deep breath... and out. Again. There's a wheeze both sides when you breathe out. No crackles. Ankles aren't swollen, no fluid there.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): So what's the verdict? Don't dance around it.

[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm tossing a few things around out loud so you can hear my thinking: the tail of that chest infection could still be irritating things, and the long smoking plus these blow-test numbers make me think of COPD, the chronic smoking-related lung disease. I'm not calling heart failure from what I see today, and I'm not locking a final label until we repeat the test when you're well clear of the infection. Working impression, though, is COPD.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): COPD. Fantastic. My old man had lung cancer, smoked like a chimney. That's all I can think about.

[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hear that, and I'm sorry. A chest X-ray is the right next step, I'll book one, not because I think it's cancer, but so we're not guessing. And we'll repeat the spirometry in about six weeks.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks of this?

[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hopefully clearer. In the meantime, the blue puffer, keep using it when you're puffed, two puffs. The purple one, even though we're not a hundred percent which brand, try to use it every day the way the chemist meant, morning and night, not just when you remember.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. No promises.

[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the smokes, I can refer you to Quitline, they'll ring you, no lecture from me. There's patches and that down the track if you want them later, not today unless you ask.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't send me patches. The phone call, fine, whatever.

[SEG0069] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll put the Quitline referral through. Come back and see me in six weeks with the repeat blow test. If you're getting more short of breath, or any blood, don't wait, come sooner or go to emergency.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah.
[SEG0071] person_3 (DOCTOR): And you're still working, or retired? Dust, fumes, any of that, just so I know the background.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Retired panel beater. Years of dust and paint. Gave it up at sixty. Still have a beer most nights, nothing wild.
[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks. That dust plus the smokes is worth knowing. Anything else you wanted to get off your chest, so to speak?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Just fix the cough. And tell that waiting room to get a better telly.
[SEG0075] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll pass it on. We'll get the X-ray form to the front desk before you go. Look after yourself, Mr Hale.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. See you in six weeks, I suppose.

spec.situation: Long-term smoker with morning cough and breathlessness; minimises smoking ('about ten a day... maybe twenty'), inhalers used irregularly, a recent chest infection; spirometry numbers read aloud; quitting support offered.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Current purple preventer used a couple times weekly supported; exact dose 2 puffs not certain, patient says maybe one or two.
bad.text: purple inhaler (dose=2 puffs, frequency=a couple of times a week, indication=preventer, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Spirometry was completed, but not requested by nurse in transcript.
Spirometry completed is supported; nurse as responsible person not established.

omissions.text: Oxygen saturation was 94% on air/room air.
Recent chest infection occurred a few weeks ago and was described by the patient as a 'proper chest infection'.
Amoxicillin course was finished last Tuesday.
The patient first denied wheeze, then corrected himself to say he does have night-time wheeze when lying flat that wakes him; this reversal/disagreement in the history is not recorded as such.
Negative finding: no wheeze initially reported when specifically asked.
The patient said he has been 'living on' Ventolin this month, indicating increased reliever use.
The purple inhaler record is inaccurate: the patient said the dose is uncertain ('maybe two puffs, might be one, I never look'), not definitely 2 puffs.
Reason for poor adherence to the purple inhaler: he hates the taste and feels it makes him cough more, so he skips it.
Doctor assessment included that heart failure was not supported by today's findings ('I'm not calling heart failure from what I see today').
Doctor stated he was not locking in a final diagnosis until spirometry is repeated when the patient is well clear of infection.
Chest X-ray was planned specifically not because the doctor thinks it is cancer, but to avoid guessing.
Safety-netting was broader than recorded: if getting more short of breath, or any blood, the patient should come sooner or go to emergency.

Occupational exposure timing is slightly wrong in the record: the patient said he retired panel beating at age 60 and is now retired, but at SEG0072 he said he 'gave it up at sixty' after years of dust and paint exposure.
